articles.body:
For different reasons, Alexander Zverev and Ben Shelton will look back on their 2026 Grand Slam performances with a sense of achievement - no matter what happens in Sunday's US Open men's final.

German top seed Zverev has emerged from the shadow of Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz to win the Grand Slam title many felt he might never land.

American eighth seed Shelton, meanwhile, has demonstrated he does have what it takes to reach a major final - and beat the world's very best players on the way.

"For me, this whole tournament has been uncharted territory," said Shelton, who will be backed by a partisan 24,000-strong crowd in New York.

"I'm in positions I've never been in before. I've beaten guys I've never beaten before."

Shelton must also beat Zverev for the first time, having lost all five of their previous meetings, if he is to become the first American man in 23 years to win a Grand Slam singles title.

At the start of the season, the odds on Zverev winning two Grand Slam titles would have been long. They are considerably shorter now.

The French Open champion is a slight favourite to beat Shelton as he looks to double his tally of major wins - not only for the year, but his career.

After three defeats in major finals, many thought the 29-year-old had missed his chance to win one of the sport's biggest prizes given how Sinner and Alcaraz - who swept the Grand Slams in 2024 and 2025 and together earned the 'Sincaraz' tag - have dominated.

But injuries to the standout pair - Alcaraz missing the French Open and Wimbledon, with Sinner ruled out of the US Open - have opened the door for someone else to make a push.

Asked if he thought he could end 2026 with more major wins than them, Zverev said: "I believed in it. I believed that it's possible. I think not many of you guys did.

"I think the question was always: Is Carlos and Jannik going to play all four Grand Slam finals between each other again?

"Of course, it was a very legit question with how the last two years went. I'm happy with how this year went so far, but I've got another big match on Sunday."

Zverev is contesting his second US Open final, having squandered a two-set lead against Dominic Thiem in 2020 - a gutting defeat that cut deep.

In the seasons that followed, Zverev often played in the latter stages at Slams with the demeanour of a man who lacked belief that his time would ever come.

His mental misgivings were finally put to bed by beating Italy's Flavio Cobolli in the final at Roland Garros and, after finishing runner-up to Sinner at Wimbledon, he has now reached a third successive Grand Slam final.

A below-par Zverev ground through the opening rounds at Flushing Meadows in a series of early-morning finishes, but he gradually improved over a fortnight where he has not yet faced a top-20 opponent.

Shelton will present a considerable step up in quality but, like Cobolli, is another opponent who may feel the weight of occasion too difficult to bear.

How to follow US Open men's final on the BBC

The significance of reaching a first US Open final has not escaped Shelton's notice.

Shelton, 23, is bidding to become the first home US Open men's singles champion since Andy Roddick in 2003 and could also become the first black American man to win a singles major since Arthur Ashe in 1975.

When a reporter said after his semi-final win over Frances Tiafoe that there was a "lot of history" on the line, a grinning Shelton replied: "Is there?"

Former world number four James Blake believes a Shelton win would be huge for African-American representation in the sport.

"Having another black American in the final leaves you wondering how many kids and adults are watching that maybe wouldn't have been otherwise," Blake told BBC Sport.

"They are going to be inspired to hear Ben's story and see someone that looks like them out there playing and competing in a sport that has historically been dominated by the sense of a country club white sport."

Known for a thunderous serve which has topped 140mph over the past fortnight, Shelton has complemented his attacking instincts by developing his defensive skills and improving his weaker backhand.

Shelton's progress has led to four title victories this season - Dallas (indoor hard), Munich (clay), Stuttgart (grass) and Canadian Open (outdoor hard) - and a watershed win over Alcaraz at the US Open.

Shelton had never beaten a top-three opponent until overcoming the seven-time champion, who was playing in his first tournament for almost five months, in an epic quarter-final which ended at 3:34am.

"Ben has been trending in the right direction throughout this year. I think four titles on different surfaces is evidence of it," Shelton's father and coach Bryan said.

"He's willing to suffer a little bit in the rallies, go deeper and really use his athleticism."

articles.body:
2026 has been the year of Elena Rybakina.

The Kazakhstani star claimed her second Grand Slam title of the season on Saturday evening after defeating Aryna Sabalenka in the US Open final .

Rybakina was almost unplayable from the baseline, striking 33 total winners during the match.

With the US Open Women's Singles event now concluded, let's take a look at the brand new WTA top 10.

Elena Rybakina becomes the new world number one, Elina Svitolina rises in the WTA rankings

Elena Rybakina was the big winner in New York, as she has walked away from the tournament with the world number one ranking.

The 27-year-old snatched the top spot from Aryna Sabalenka after defeating Qinwen Zheng in the US Open quarter-finals.

Rybakina went on to defeat Coco Gauff and Sabalenka to claim the title, solidifying her status as the best player on the planet.

Elina Svitolina also rose two spots in the rankings, despite only reaching the third round in New York.

Svitolina's rise had as much to do with the Ukrainian's results as it did with Iga Swiatek and Karolina Muchova's disappointing campaigns.

Both players fell one spot in the rankings after losing in the fourth round and third round, respectively.

On a more positive note, Marta Kostyuk has made her top 10 debut after reaching the fourth round in New York.

Elena Rybakina emulates Victoria Azarenka

Rybakina defeated two former US Open champions en route to winning her first title in Flushing Meadows.

The Kazakhstani first beat Coco Gauff: the 2023 champion.

She then triumphed against Aryna Sabalenka: the two-time defending champion in New York.

In defeating these two players, Rybakina has become the first player to defeat former women's singles champions in the semi-final and final of a Grand Slam event since Victoria Azarenka, according to OptaAce .

Azarenka accomplished the feat at the 2012 Australian Open, defeating Kim Clijsters in the semi-finals and Maria Sharapova in the final.

Clijsters won the 2011 Australian Open, while Sharapova captured the title in 2008.

articles.summary: Tennis News: NEW YORK CITY: Elena Rybakina’s US Open appeared to have ended before it had begun.A foot and ankle injury in Cincinnati saw the Kazakh limp out of th.
articles.body: NEW YORK CITY: Elena Rybakina’s US Open appeared to have ended before it had begun.A foot and ankle injury in Cincinnati saw the Kazakh limp out of the tournament midway, leaving her Flushing Meadows dream in tatters and her pursuit of the world No. 1 ranking suddenly hanging by a thread.Rybakina took a week off, giving her left foot time to heal.When she kickstarted her campaign in New York ten days later, she began cautiously, testing her foot, especially on her serve, the shot most troubled by the injury. By Saturday afternoon, caution had turned into conviction.A remarkable display of mental and physical resilience carried Rybakina to her first US Open crown, a 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 win over Aryna Sabalenka, the powerful Belarusian, and her third Grand Slam title.And by the end of it, the woman who had spent the past 24 months negotiating upheaval was sitting atop the tennis world.“I always believed that it's possible,” she said, her expression joyful. Smiles punctuating her sentences.She had won Wimbledon in 2022 and reached the Australian Open final the following year, but there was no Grand Slam title.“I feel like now I have a great team, great people around me, and we just continue the work. It finally paid off, and I'm super happy, very proud.”In her coaching corner is 39-year-old Croat Stefano Vukov and Stanislav Khmarskyi, who joined the setup as co-coach in 2025. Italian Aldo Chiari, is her strength and conditioning coach and Adam Jones is her hitting partner.Vukov, the most audible of her bench courtside, was banned from the Tour for eight months (January 2025 to August) for a breach of the code of conduct regarding his behaviour toward Rybakina.The Kazakh began the 2025 season working with Goran Ivanisevic and later signed on Davide Sanguinetti, a friend of Vukov’s. Yet Vukov remained a constant presence in her tennis life away from the cameras.At the 2025 WTA Finals, she declined a photo with WTA CEO Portia Archer demonstrating her displeasure over the suspension of Vukov. Archer later resigned, and Rybakina's rise to No. 1 has added another layer to a relationship and a period that has often played out under intense scrutiny.Through it all, Rybakina kept playing.And now she has done more than simply return to the top. She has built the most complete season of her career, winning the WTA Finals (2025), the Australian Open and the US Open while becoming world No. 1.“I feel like this tournament was more stressful because I was playing for No. 1, and then, of course, this injury which happened the week before,” she said. “So every day was kind of a challenge, but I felt like in these situations I was more calm than when similar things were happening, like, before.”Even in the final, with the title within touching distance, the nerves came.Serving for the championship, Rybakina hit two double faults before closing out the match with her 12th ace. It was an appropriate snapshot of the evening, pressure, risk, then the nerve to trust her biggest weapon when it mattered most.“On the other side is a great player, and she can go for her shots and that I actually need to win it myself. Yeah, I feel it was just a lot of pressure, nerves.”Rybakina is already looking beyond the celebration, even if the next target is obvious. A career Grand Slam is now within sight, with the French Open the only major missing from her collection.“Well, the main priority, as I was saying before, I'm not getting younger, is try to keep myself healthy and definitely choose the calendar correctly,” she said.“The goal is always the biggest tournaments, you want to win them,.”She has climbed from the brink of missing the US Open to winning it, from No. 2 to No. 1, from a year of uncertainty to a season of remarkable success.And yet, for Rybakina, the climb is not finished.“Yeah, we will see what's going to happen, but definitely it's still a lot of work to do,” she said. “The job is never done, to be honest.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Elena Rybakina's US Open title run puts her on top of women's tennis and Sabalenka has work to do
articles.summary: Elena Rybakina was going to see her name on top of the women's tennis rankings Monday no matter what happened in the U.S. Open final.  Rybakina was too good...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Elena Rybakina was going to see her name on top of the women's tennis rankings Monday no matter what happened in the U.S. Open final .

Still, it wouldn't have felt quite the same to pass Aryna Sabalenka and become No. 1 in a tournament where Sabalenka then beat Rybakina to defend her title. It would not only have been confusing to casual fans, but a letdown to the player.

Nothing to worry about there. Rybakina was too good for Sabalenka and anyone else in the sport right now, so her 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 victory Sunday triggered a dual celebration.

"I feel that it's going to be amazing to wake up knowing that you achieved such big things," Rybakina said.

There could be more to come. The 27-year-old who was born in Russia but represents Kazakhstan is on top of her game, with two Grand Slam titles in 2026. She beat Sabalenka in both finals , and even the former No. 1 concedes it would be tough to get back to the top if Rybakina stays at the level she displayed in Flushing Meadows.

"She continues to play like that, then yeah, I'm in trouble," Sabalenka said.

The 28-year-old from Belarus had won the previous two U.S. Open titles, appeared in three straight finals and reached at least the semifinals every year since 2021. Rybakina, meanwhile, had never even gotten past the fourth round before this year.

"For some reason, New York wasn't my best place for tennis for the past years," Rybakina said, "but definitely now it changed."

So much has at the top of women's tennis.

It began toward the end of 2025, when Rybakina beat Sabalenka for the title at the season-ending WTA Finals . Then it was the same result at the Australian Open final, and Rybakina has gone on to match Sabalenka and French Open winner Mirra Andreeva with a tour-high three titles. Her 49 victories are one behind No. 3 Jessica Pegula for tops this year.

"I always believed that it's possible," Rybakina said. "We've been having great results. Of course, not every year is the same. I won Wimbledon in 2022. Then I wasn't winning the Slams, but I played the final of the Australian Open the next year. I think we were always there.

"I feel like now I have a great team, great people around me, and we just continue the work. It finally paid off."

Rybakina played so well over the past year — and Sabalenka struggled this summer — that she was assured of accumulating enough points to move up from No. 2 if she reached the semifinals at the U.S. Open. Perhaps the only thing that could have prevented that was a foot injury that Rybakina sustained at the Cincinnati Open. She stopped playing in her quarterfinal match against Iga Swiatek and then couldn't get back on the court for a few days.

So Rybakina had a lot weighing on her mind in New York, but it never seemed to affect her tennis.

"I feel like this tournament was just kind of more stressful because I was playing for No. 1 one of the matches, and then, of course, this injury which happened the week before," Rybakina said. "So every day was kind of a challenge, but I felt like in these situations I was more calm than when similar things were happening before."

She now needs only the French Open title to complete the career Grand Slam, and that one always figured to be the toughest to get because the red clay slows her powerful shots in ways that hard courts and grass can't.

There will surely be more meetings at the big events with Sabalenka, who held the No. 1 ranking for 99 consecutive weeks.

"Ninety-nine?" Sabalenka said. "Well, that's amazing. Let's see if Elena can beat me in that," she said with a laugh.

Sabalenka still leads their rivalry 10-8, and they have split four meetings this year. But Rybakina won the matches that mattered most.

"I don't know what future will bring, but it's always very difficult matches against Aryna, and I feel like we push each other to be better after such tough battles," Rybakina said.

"I don't know what future is going to bring, but I hope success and some more wins."

articles.summary: El alemán, de 29 años, derrota a Shelton en cuatro sets y deja sin título del US Open a Estados Unidos
articles.body: La central Arthur Ashe llenó el domingo las 23.000 localidades esperando ver ganar a un tenista local por primera vez en 23 años. Toparon con una cruda realidad. Alexander Zverev es mucho mejor que Ben Shelton. Lo dice el resultado de la final (6-3, 7-6 y 7-6) y 6-2, y lo decían las estadísticas previas. Los cinco precedentes entre ambos habían caído del lado del alemán, que encadenaba 10 sets. Gracias a su coronación en junio sobre la tierra de Roland Garros, Zverev es otro, más liberado y con menos presión. Ahora nunca hubiese perdido el duelo neoyorquino de 2020 con Dominic Thiem después de anotarse las dos primeras mangas. El vencedor estaba tan nervioso que no se dio cuenta que había ganado tras la consecución del octavo juego del cuarto set y se dispuso a restar. Sólo el ruido del público le hizo saber de su victoria. Desde Andy Roddick, en 2003, ningún americano ha estado ni cerca de levantar el trofeo. No lo estuvieron Andre Agassi y Roddick, en las ediciones de 2005 y 2006 que cedieron ante Roger Federer. Y tampoco Taylor Fritz en la final de hace dos campañas frente a Jannik Sinner. Han pasado 8.407 días desde el éxito de 'A-Rod' y más que van a pasar. Shelton por perder, perdió hasta el primer servicio del partido. Si no era fiable con su mejor arma, no tenía nada que hacer. En la semifinal con su compatriota Frances Tiafoe había establecido el saque más veloz en la historia de los Grand Slam. Pero los nervios de una gran final son otra cosa. Estaba pagando la novatada. Sascha, como todo el vestuario del circuito masculino, conoce el agujero que tiene el zurdo de Atlanta con su revés. Hacia ese lado le tiraba insistentemente el alemán. El ruido, ya de por sí ensordecedor de la central del Billie Jean King Tennis Center, era menos gracias a que la lluvia dio una tregua y se pudo jugar con el techo abierto. Nadie ha ganado más partidos que Zverev en 2026, con 53, de los que 25 corresponden a los 'majors'. Es el décimo tenista que hace valer su condición de primer favorito del cuadro en la Era Open (1968). La consecución del tie break del segundo set aceleró el desenlace por mucho que Shelton se fue a perder el tiempo al vestuario. Es difícil ganar una final si no dispones de una sola pelota de rotura hasta las 2 horas y 19 minutos de juego. Ben, inferior desde el fondo de la pista, pasó al ataque total con constantes subidas a la red. La nueva táctica tuvo premio porque a su rival empezó a darle eso del miedo escénico. En el tenis hay que proponer y el de Hamburgo no estaba ofreciendo nada. Le salvó un primer 'break' en el inicio del cuarto asalto, que le ayudó a templar sus nervios. El americano se había quedado sin tenis y gasolina.

articles.title: Alexander Zverev doesn't realize he'd won US Open, keeps America waiting yet another year
articles.summary: The 23-year drought since an American male has won a tennis major will extend into a 24th after Zverev topped Shelton.
articles.body:
NEW YORK — How much did the crowd at Arthur Ashe Stadium want American Ben Shelton to win the US Open? This much: the cheers trying to rally Shelton to victory were even louder than those for the crowd shots of Jalen Brunson, Karl-Anthony Towns and the rest of the world champion Knicks on the stadium video boards. That's how you know you've got New York in your corner.

Unfortunately for Shelton, the Arthur Ashe crowd couldn't help him land his second serves, target his volleys, or figure a way past Alexander Zverev. Shelton, the latest American man seeking to end a Grand Slam-less streak that will extend into its 24th year, simply could not get past Zverev, no matter how hard the crowd pushed him.

"I'm going to need you guys on Sunday to bring the energy," Shelton said on Friday night after defeating fellow American Francis Tiafoe. "I'm going for it here. I'm going to leave it all on the court. I hope you guys come and back me. Let's do this for the USA." They did indeed bring the energy, but it wasn't nearly enough.

There was a moment where the match could have turned out differently, when Shelton finally broke Zverev in the 34th game of the match to win the third set. For the first time in the match, the smirky smile that has become Shelton's signature actually meant something.

Hope flickered for a brief moment … and then Zverev broke right back to begin the fourth set, and from there cruised to a 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2 victory. So locked in was Zverev that when he served out Shelton to win the match and the title, he didn't even realize he'd won, making for an amusing ending.

For more than a decade, the now 29-year-old Zverev was the individual player who most felt the pinch of all those majors going to the Big Three of Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic, and then the Big Two in Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz. Despite seven semis and three finals appearances, he'd never won a Grand Slam. But he finally broke through at Roland-Garros earlier this year, and now has a second.

For Zverev, it turned out to only be a matter of time. And time is what's looming now over the American men — the decades of time since any of them have managed to break through and win just one Grand Slam event. No Wimbledon. No Roland-Garros. No Australian. No hometown tourney. Not since Andy Roddick won here in 2003 has an American man won. And in tennis, the flag on one side of your name is almost as important as your score on the other.

Much like the World Cup, where the Americans also fall short on the global stage year after year, the tennis drought is almost inexplicable. How can America produce so many tennis players, so many champions, and not one men's tennis champion?

Unlike the World Cup, however, American men will have four more opportunities to claim that elusive next Grand Slam next year, starting in just a few months in Australia. The natural assumption would be that if the American men just keep kicking at the door, they'll eventually bust through … but in this case, the natural assumption might well be wrong.

If Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner regain their health and their form, and if Zverev continues to ascend, they'll combine for an imposing barrier for anyone trying to break through. Ask any American player — Mardy Fish, John Isner, Sam Querrey, James Blake — what it was like playing in the Nadal/Federer/Djokovic era, and the story always ends the same way.

Ironically, the 23-year-old Shelton provides a bit of ammunition for those who insist that America would dominate any sport, but our best athletes insist on playing football or basketball. Shelton came late to the game, initially thinking his 6-foot-4 height and preternatural athleticism would be a better fit for football. He didn't proceed through America's youth tennis-industrial complex, instead learning the game from his father. He possesses the rare combination of skill, grace and charisma that separates the great from the very good.

The question now for him is whether he'll be able to capitalize on the opportunity that lies ahead of him. This year's US Open marked uncharted territory for Shelton. He's never before reached the finals of a Grand Slam event, falling in the semifinals of the US Open in 2023 and the Australian Open in 2025. And Shelton has been inconsistent on the Grand Slam stages; in 2026 alone he has everything from a first-round exit at Wimbledon to this finals appearance. Will this experience help him reach the next rung on the ladder, or will he take another step back? We'll have to wait until the Australian Open in January to start learning that answer.

Roddick, for his part, isn't celebrating his standing as the last American man to win a Grand Slam. Anything but.

"At this point, I hate talking about it," he said on his "Served" podcast last year. "I get asked about it all the time. I'm not the '72 Dolphins. I don't pop champagne when someone's perfect season is gone. I want this so much, probably more than anyone outside the people who are going to end up winning it."

There's an old truism in Formula 1 racing — another international sport where the United States has failed to dominate — that catching an opponent is one thing, passing them is quite another. For so many years, American men weren't able to even catch the dominant leaders of men's tennis. Shelton has, at least, managed to get on their level. The challenge now is learning how to climb past them.

articles.summary: Shelton entered his first Grand Slam final hoping to end a drought of more than 20 years for American men at the New York tournament.
articles.body: German star Alexander Zverev overtook Ben Shelton to win the U.S. Open on Sunday, securing his second Grand Slam title and evaporating dreams of an American man winning the title for the first time in more than 20 years. The score was 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2. After the match, Zverev accepted the Tiffany & Co. trophy from American tennis great Jimmy Connors and $5.5 million in prize money. He thanked his mother for getting him through a diabetes diagnosis at age 4 and letting him know he could prevail. “If he wants to be a tennis player, he’ll be a tennis player,” Zverev said, quoting her. “My mother is the most important and strongest person I know.” Shelton thanked God and said the experience was positive regardless of the outcome. “My successes are a gift, the failures are a gift, and being here playing in front of you guys is a gift,” he said. Girlfriend Trinity Rodman was in the stands wearing a Shelton shirt. Rodman, a professional soccer player for the Washington Spirit, started in her team’s 3-0 loss to the Boston Legacy at home Sunday but managed to also support Shelton in New York. It was a thrilling final in Arthur Ashe Stadium between two men with powerful serves and something to prove on one of tennis’ biggest stages. Shelton lagged early in the first set, struggling to make headway against Zverev’s methodical approach. But Shelton began gaining ground against the more experienced Zverev, growing more confident in his returns and catching him off guard with well-timed forehands. He pushed Zverev to a tiebreaker in the second set but ultimately fell short, entering the third set well behind. Shelton dug deep to push Zverev in the third set, rattling him as he crawled out from the two-set deficit he found himself in. In the fourth and final set, Zverev was hit with a time violation, and he protested it to no avail. The moment did not derail him, and he went up 3-1 and stayed ahead, breaking Shelton’s serve to make it 5-2 before cruising to victory on serve. It was the first appearance in a Grand Slam final for Shelton, 23, but Zverev, 29, is well acquainted with the pressure of a major final. He had played in five Grand Slam finals before Sunday’s match. Zverev came into the tournament in Queens with momentum from winning the French Open in June. He endured two difficult matches to open the tournament but did not drop a set on his way to the final after the second round. Shelton, on the other hand, fought two-time U.S. Open champion Carlos Alcaraz for 4 hours and 28 minutes for a place in the semifinals. It was a grueling match that started late Tuesday and ended at 3:33 a.m. Wednesday. Shelton pushed Alcaraz to the limit as Alcaraz competed in his first major since having injured his wrist. Alcaraz appeared to vomit into a towel at one point. Shelton then defeated fellow American Frances Tiafoe on Friday night, dominating in a 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 victory. In the final, Shelton had a shot at becoming the first American man to win the U.S. Open since Andy Roddick in 2003, defeating Spain’s Juan Carlos Ferrero. Fans in the stadium were raucous in their support for him. Some told NBC News that they had traveled from near and far. Many were hoping that Shelton could become the second Black man to win the U.S. Open. The only other player to have accomplished that was Arthur Ashe, the namesake of the court on which Sunday’s final was played, in 1968. Tracie Saundera told NBC News before the match that she was excited to see a Black man in the final, especially considering the last time it happened, in 1972, was before she was born. Shelton is also simply an exciting player to watch, she added. “He just plays with so much passion and energy,” Saundera said. “He’s so fun to watch play, and he’s young and enthusiastic. ... I’m old. Most of my players are retiring, so it’s good to see some of the young kids coming in and just being powerhouses.” University of Florida fan Junior Pulayya drove from Florida to New York to support Shelton, an alumnus of the school. He noted that there had been a drought of “really solid” American men’s players until now. “But this is, just, it gets that new generation of kids that follow tennis, that get involved in tennis, that want to get involved in tennis,” Pulayya said. “It does so much just for today, but long term for the sport.” Longtime tennis fan Shameka Littles, of Maryland, said she could not imagine how it felt for Shelton to play on the Arthur Ashe court as the first Black man to make the U.S. Open final in more than 50 years. But beyond that, Littles said, it was “inspiring” to see so many Americans do well this year. “To have so many of the top seeds, you know, make it to the semifinals, the quarterfinals — that was exciting in and of itself,” she said. “Hopefully, it just kind of gives, you know, a big boost of energy and excitement for each other.”

articles.title: Men’s top seed Alexander Zverev caps breakthrough year with US Open title
articles.summary: Men’s top seed Alexander Zverev won a thrilling four-set, three hour and 33 minute showdown with No. 8 seed Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2 to win his first career US Open title on Sunday.
articles.body: Men’s top seed Alexander Zverev won a thrilling four-set, three-hour and 33 minute showdown with No. 8 seed Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2 to win his first career US Open title on Sunday. It is the second career grand slam win for the 29-year-old from Germany, with his first coming at Roland Garros earlier this year. Zverev’s triumph further extends the grand slam drought for American men at least another year. After morning rain plagued the New York metropolitan area earlier in the day, the roof at Arthur Ashe Stadium was open and ready for the battle between the two. However, the first set was Zverev’s comfortably. The German jumped out to a 3-1 lead, and Shelton couldn’t keep up despite his usual strong serves that seem to give many trouble. Zverev took the set 6-3. The second set proved to be more difficult for Zverev, with the 23-year-old Shelton continuing to respond to everything he did. Earlier this week, the 29-year-old Zverev was asked about his lengthy bouncing of the balls before serves which he claimed he did not do it “on purpose.” Well, things got testy as Shelton complained to the chair umpire about Zverev’s antics ahead of his serves. No penalty or warning was ultimately assessed. The pressure on Zverev did not let up with Shelton eventually forcing a tiebreak, but the German jumped out to a rapid 5-0 lead and eventually would win the set 7-6 (2). Shelton showed his mettle in the third set, and the New York crowd came to life. The American quickly ran up to a 4-3 lead but Zverev showed no quit, with both players going back-and-forth. But it was Shelton who won the third frame 7-5, avoiding a straight-set defeat. Just as the crowd was back into it with a majority behind Shelton, it was Zverev that overcame the momentum swing and dispatched Shelton 6-2 in a comfortable fourth set to cap off a career year. After Shelton failed to return serve on championship point, Zverev didn’t seem to initially realize he had clinched the win. After a few seconds, he went into celebration mode and let out a huge “lets go” to his box. Zverev finishes his year with a 25-2 in majors and is taking home won $5.5 million, the same prize earned by women’s singles champion Elena Rybakina on Saturday as the largest in Grand Slam history. Zverev knew he was not the crowd favorite but still thanked them for the support the last two weeks. “It was an incredible atmosphere to play in, even though the crowd was against me. You guys brought the energy and noise,” Zverev said. Shelton’s girlfriend and soccer star, Trinity Rodman, who had a game earlier Sunday with her National Women’s Soccer League (NWSL) team Washington Spirit, was able to make it from Washington DC to catch the ending of the match. Zverev joked, “Trinity, I thought you had a game today, no? Well done to you as well. You’re the lucky charm. … Not today, but usually.” Shelton came up short in his quest to become the first American man to win the tournament since Andy Roddick did so in 2003. He was also aiming to become the first Black male tennis player to win it since Arthur Ashe in 1968. “My successes are a gift, my failures are a gift. Playing in front of you guys is a gift,” Shelton told the crowd after the match. “I have the best support team in the business. To do this with my family by my side, these four guys over here who dedicate their life to my career, spend time travelling the world with me, it’s an unnatural commitment. I appreciate you guys.” Shelton ended by saying, “I’m just getting started, I’ll be back here again.” This story has been updated with the latest information.

articles.summary: Alexander Zverev's fantastic 2026 continued in earnest on Sunday.
articles.body:
Alexander Zverev's fantastic 2026 continued in earnest on Sunday.

Zverev earned his second Grand Slam title in his career—both this season—after defeating Ben Shelton in four sets, 6-3, 7-6, 5-7, 6-2, during the U.S. Open final.

It was the expected result—Zverev was the top overall seed and was playing in his third straight Grand Slam final this season after winning the French Open and losing to Jannik Sinner in the Wimbledon final.

Shelton, meanwhile, was the U.S. Open's No. 8 seed, and his run to the final included a quarterfinal upset over Carlos Alcaraz.

In a tournament full of memorable moments, Zverev provided a few more:

And Zverev was so locked in he barely realized he won once the match was over:

The 29-year-old didn't exactly have the most difficult run to his second Grand Slam title, playing just one opponent seeded in the top 20 while avoiding players like Alcaraz and Novak Djokovic. But he had no control over the rest of the field.

Still, until he proves he can regularly knock off Alcaraz and Sinner in the biggest tournaments, he likely isn't going to crack the conversation of top men's player. He's 6-7 all-time against Alcaraz (2-3 in Grand Slams) but just 4-11 against Sinner (2-3 in Grand Slams).

Reaching every Grand Slam final at least once in the past two seasons, however, is a good indication that he's at least knocking on that door. And he didn't allow Shelton to fight back against him, closing the door in the fourth set after the young American showed his fight.

The tennis world still revolves around Sinner and Alcaraz when the pair are healthy. But Zverev saw the field open up favorably for him in New York and didn't let his moment pass.

articles.body: El Abierto de los Estados Unidos ha celebrado su cierre, con la final masculina, sin ningún tipo de contratiempo más allá de la mala climatología.Todo lo contrario que en la pasada edición, donde el partido decisivo entre Carlos Alcaraz y Jannik Sinner, estuvo eclipsado por la presencia del presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump. Por él se retrasó la final media hora y por él se montaron unas colas kilométricas en los puntos de acceso al estadio por las medidas extraordinarias de seguridad. La conclusión es que más de 7.000 aficionados se sentaron en su localidad media hora después de iniciarse la acción. Trump se perdió el viernes los actos conmemorativos del 11-S y el tenis porque este fin de semana sus planes estaban reservados al golf, que es el deporte que más le gusta y que más practica. De hecho se le ha podido ver siguiendo con atención las jornadas del Open de Irlanda. Los asistentes a las finales, tanto femenina como masculina, se llevan como regalo a casa una gorra oficial del torneo que es repartida en los vomitorios de entrada por parte de voluntarios de la organización. Zverev ha ganado su segundo título de Grand Slam jugando los siete partidos con el reloj de la firma firma neoyorquina Jacob & Co. valorado en más de 20.000 euros. El modelo en cuestión es el Epic X Black Titanium, fabricado en titanio con revestimiento DLC negro y correa de caucho. No es el único tenista que juega con reloj. En el tenis español recurre a él Dani Mérida. El madrileño disputa sus partidos con un Gerald Charles. Su precio va desde los 17.000 euros a los 60.000. No hay final de Grand Slam en la que no esté el actor Brad Pitt y su pareja, Inés de Ramón. Estuvieron en junio en Roland Garros y no han faltado a las finales femenina y masculina del Abierto de los Estados Unidos. El mismo fanatismo por el tenis tiene la editora de Vogue, Anna Wintour. También ha repetido este fin de semana la cantante Pink. Otro rostro conocido fue el del compositor, Lin-Manuel Miranda y el de Pierce Brosnan. En Nueva York conviven estos días el tenis con la semana de la moda. Y todo el mundo que se precie se deja ver por la ciudad. La cantidad de veces que hace botar la pelota Zverev en el momento del saque es para desesperarse. La jueza de silla le advirtió hasta que le señalizó un warning en el cuarto juego del cuarto set, con un marcador favorable de 2-1.

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Alexander Zverev beats Ben Shelton for second Grand Slam title
articles.summary: Alexander Zverev lands his second Grand Slam title after ending Ben Shelton's hopes of becoming a rare home US Open men's champion.
articles.body:
Alexander Zverev used his greater experience to beat home hope Ben Shelton in the US Open final and quiet a partisan crowd hoping to laud a rare American men's champion.

German top seed Zverev lifted a heavy burden by winning his first major title at this year's French Open and has quickly added another with a 6-3 7-6 (7-2) 5-7 6-2 victory over Shelton in New York.

At the start of the season, there were question marks over whether 29-year-old Zverev would ever win one of the sport's most prestigious prizes.

Now he is celebrating becoming a multiple Grand Slam singles champion, having seen the path to glory partially cleared by injuries to Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz.

Sinner and Alcaraz swept the board between them at the majors in 2024 and 2025 - and Zverev has taken full advantage against the rest of the field in their absences.

Big-hitting Shelton, 23, has long been identified as a player who can win the biggest titles, but ultimately came up short in his first Grand Slam final against a rejuvenated Zverev.

Eighth seed Shelton was aiming to become the first American man to win a major singles title since Andy Roddick in 2003, but losing serve in the first game of the match set the tone as Zverev controlled the opening two sets.

The momentum shifted in the third set, however, as Shelton finally started applying serious pressure on Zverev's serve.

Taking his third break opportunity provided encouragement to the 24,000 home fans on Arthur Ashe Stadium, but starting the fourth set with a poor service game allowed Zverev to reassert his authority and extinguish American dreams.

Zverev did not initially know he had secured victory when Shelton hit a return long on championship point, only breaking out into a broad and slightly surprised smile after his team pointed out the score to him.

All About US Open: Zverev claims second Grand Slam title

Zverev uses Grand Slam-winning experience to see off Shelton

Going into the 2026 season, few people would have backed Zverev to win two Grand Slam tournaments, with the German having already lost three major finals in a career which looked in danger of not living up to expectation.

But injuries to his biggest rivals - Alcaraz missing the French Open and Wimbledon, with Sinner ruled out of the US Open - opened the door for Zverev.

A below-par Zverev scraped through the opening rounds at Flushing Meadows in a series of early-morning finishes, but he gradually improved over a fortnight where he did not play a top-20 opponent until Shelton.

Zverev had not lost to Shelton in their five previous meetings and immediately capitalised on a nervy start by his opponent.

Shelton double-faulted on break point in the first game of the match, handing over the type of initiative that opponents often struggle to wrestle back from Zverev.

Through the strength of his first serve, and his ability to unpick Shelton's weaker backhand in the baseline exchanges, Zverev rolled through the opening set and clinched it when Shelton hit another double fault on set point.

Zverev continued to patiently draw mistakes from Shelton in the second set, but without being gifted a break when his only opportunity arrived in the fourth game.

He instead showed why he has a strong tie-break record with another nerveless display and, unlike in the 2020 US Open final when he lost from a two-set lead, kept his composure in the pressure moments to secure a commanding victory.

Addressing his team which is led by his father Alexander senior and brother Mischa, Zverev said: "We went 30 years without winning a Grand Slam title and now won two in the span of three months.

"I think God has seen how hard we have worked, how hard we have suffered and how much pain we went through.

"I think 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before."

Positives for Shelton - but work still to do

Despite the bitter disappointment of losing Sunday's showpiece, Shelton will take pride from his run to a first major final, as well as further belief he can win a Grand Slam title.

Shelton came into the tournament with confidence after winning the Canadian Open last month, but also with a point to prove after an underwhelming season at the Grand Slams.

A chastening first-round exit at Wimbledon against Finnish qualifier Otto Virtanen was described by Shelton as "one of the toughest losses" of his career, acting as a wake-up call going into the North American hard court swing.

He has bounced back superbly to come close to ending America's 23-year wait for somebody to finally follow in Roddick's footsteps.

Shelton did not have an easy route to the final, needing to overcome a series of big-hitting opponents which included three former top-10 players as well as seven-time major champion Alcaraz.

Shelton had never beaten a top-three opponent until powering past Alcaraz - who was playing in his first tournament for almost five months - in an epic quarter-final which ended at 3:34am.

However, he could not double that tally against world number two Zverev.

Shelton's recent success has been a product of developing his defensive skills and improving his weaker backhand, but not being able to execute his damaging forehand in crucial moments against Zverev proved costly.

It was a reminder of the work the American number one still has to do at the highest level against the very best opponents.

"I'm excited with the progress that I feel that I've made, but this one stings 100%," said Shelton.

"I made too many errors when I had the ball there on my strings."

articles.title: Ben Shelton loses in US Open final to Zverev, but America has found its next big men's tennis star
articles.summary: Alexander Zverev beat Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6, 5-7, 6-2 to win the US Open, but the 23-year-old American's fight showed why fans can't wait to watch him.
articles.body: Let’s get the obvious part out of the way immediately: This stinks. Ben Shelton had a chance to end a 23-year Grand Slam drought for American men’s tennis on Sunday afternoon in New York. Instead, Alexander Zverev beat him 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2 to win the U.S. Open and capture his second Grand Slam title of the year. American men’s tennis missed a golden opportunity, but Shelton gave America a tennis star worth rooting for. It's not the same as winning, but it's a major positive step for a country desperate to find the next great American player. Ben Shelton’s nerves cost him in the U.S. Open final Shelton, making his first career Grand Slam final appearance, looked nervous from the start. The first game told us exactly what kind of afternoon this might be. He committed two errors to give Zverev an immediate break point, then double-faulted to hand over the break in the first game of the match. Shelton double-faulted again on set point to drop the opening set, 6-3. LADIES AT THE US OPEN WERE CAUGHT ON CAMERA TAKING NOTICE OF A SHIRTLESS CARLOS ALCARAZ The second set played out on even terms until the tiebreak, which is where Shelton’s game fell apart. Zverev raced to a 5-0 lead and took it 7-2. Zverev wasn’t blowing Shelton off the court, which is what made the match so frustrating to watch. Shelton kept getting into winnable points on Zverev’s serve, only to miss a forehand, dump a backhand into the net or choose the wrong shot at the wrong moment. For most of the match, Shelton looked like the more gifted player. His power, athleticism and creativity are fun to watch. The 23-year-old American produced most of the shots that made the crowd gasp and his serve regularly crossed 140 mph. His flashes of greatness showed that he's much more than another American man with a big serve. But the inconsistency killed his chances to win his first Grand Slam title. Zverev didn’t need to be spectacular. He served well, kept the ball in play and waited for Shelton to crack. Steady isn’t particularly exciting, but it wins Grand Slam finals when the guy on the other side keeps giving away points. And Zverev's win at the French Open earlier this summer gave him a crucial edge in experience that showed up throughout the match. Still, Shelton didn’t go quietly. He finally earned his first break point of the match with Zverev serving at 2-3 in the third set, but the German erased it. Shelton kept holding, waited for another chance and pounced with Zverev serving at 5-6. He jumped ahead 0-40 and converted his second set point when Zverev missed a routine volley. So, Shelton had life. Then he immediately put himself in trouble again. Shelton led 30-0 in his opening service game of the fourth set before a double fault and another forehand error opened the door. He saved one break point with a gutsy serve-and-volley play, but Zverev eventually broke and never gave it back. That was essentially the match. Zverev broke Shelton again at 4-2 before serving out the match in the final game. There was a funny moment at the very end, as Zverev didn't realize he had just won the U.S. Open. After a Shelton return went long, Zverev appeared to think there was more tennis to play. He went to serve again before realizing the match was over and he was the champion. At that point, a huge smile crept over his face and he threw his arms in the air. On the other side, a clearly frustrated Ben Shelton appeared to be holding back his emotions as he went to shake his opponent's hand. American men’s tennis let the opening slip away This was the opportunity. World No. 1 Jannik Sinner withdrew prior to the tournament because of a knee injury. Novak Djokovic lost in the first round. Shelton stunned defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set quarterfinal that ended at 3:33 in the morning. The three biggest obstacles were gone and Shelton was responsible for eliminating one of them. US OPEN WINNER ANDY RODDICK DEFENDS LATE FINISHES AMID CRITICISM AFTER BEN SHELTON-CARLOS ALCARAZ THRILLER Zverev was hardly an easy opponent. He won the French Open in June, reached the Wimbledon final and entered Sunday having beaten Shelton in all five of their previous meetings. Now the 29-year-old owns two major championships. Over the past 30 years, only seven other men have won multiple Grand Slam titles in the same calendar year: Pete Sampras, Andre Agassi, Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal, Novak Djokovic, Carlos Alcaraz and Sinner. That’s elite company. Zverev’s off-the-court legacy is more complicated. He has faced domestic abuse allegations from two former partners, both of which he has denied. The ATP closed an investigation into one set of allegations in 2023 after finding insufficient evidence to substantiate the claims, and a German court closed a separate case in 2024 after a settlement with no finding or admission of guilt. On the court, there’s no longer any debate about whether Zverev can handle the final Sunday of a major. He proved it in Paris and did it again in New York. But this was still a winnable final for Shelton. Since Andy Roddick won the 2003 U.S. Open, American men have gone 0-for-7 in Grand Slam finals. Roddick accounted for four of those losses, while Andre Agassi, Taylor Fritz and now Shelton each fell once. American men’s tennis couldn’t have asked for a clearer path to ending the drought. It still couldn’t finish the job and, because of that, it's a failure. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Ben Shelton made this run about America and God Of course, ESPN immediately tried to turn Shelton’s run into a story about race. "It’s more than just Ben Shelton’s first U.S. Open Final," the network posted after his semifinal victory. ESPN then noted that Shelton was the first Black American man to reach the U.S. Open final since Arthur Ashe in 1972. That’s historically accurate. But Shelton never made this run about his skin color. The media wanted to put him in that box, and he didn’t follow them there. He’s an American. That’s what mattered. Shelton has consistently used his platform to talk about his Christian faith, his family and his country. After winning in Australia earlier this year, he signed a television camera with the message, "USA ’til it’s backwards." After beating Alcaraz in the biggest victory of his career, Shelton immediately pointed to his faith. "I’m just so grateful, so blessed. God’s blessed me in so many ways," Shelton said. He made a similar point after winning in Montreal earlier this summer, saying, "I would be nowhere without my faith. That’s what’s most important to me." Then came Friday’s semifinal against Frances Tiafoe, played on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Shelton spoke about the sacrifices his parents made and dedicated the victory to his late grandmother. He asked the New York crowd to return for the final because, as he put it, "We’re going for it here." "Do this for the USA," Shelton said. Before leaving the court, completely unprompted, Shelton offered his thoughts and prayers to the families affected by 9/11 and called New York one of the greatest cities in the world. That’s the guy America has watched for the past two weeks. He’s powerful, emotional and wildly entertaining. He also loves his family, talks openly about God and treats representing the United States as an honor, not a burden. Now, let’s not pretend losing a Grand Slam final is the same as winning one because it isn't. Ben Shelton will be the first one to say that, too. He had the chance American men’s tennis had been waiting more than two decades to get, and he didn’t finish the job. But Shelton’s tournament was still a massive win for him and for American tennis. He showed the composure, faith and love of country that make American sports fans want to invest in a player. Shelton didn’t deliver America a trophy on Sunday. But he gave us a tennis star we can’t wait to watch try again.

Lo sucedido a la conclusión de la final masculina del US Open es lo más surrealista que se ha visto en una celebración de un título de Grand Slam. De hecho, Alexander Zverev, el vencedor, no demostró ningún tipo de alegría al ganar el octavo juego del cuarto set porque pensaba que le faltaba un juego. Supongo que me ayudó, porque, de saberlo, habría cometido tres dobles faltas en lugar de una". Fue el ruido de la grada y la presencia de Ben Shelton en la red lo que le alertó de que la final había acabado.

articles.title: US Open: Top seed Alexander Zverev ends Ben Shelton’s run and American dreams to claim title in four sets
articles.summary: Alexander Zverev adds a maiden US Open title to his French Open crown after overcoming Ben Shelton in a four-set battle; watch the Laver Cup at The O2 in London from 25-27 September live on Sky Sports.
articles.body:
The German proved too strong for the eighth-seeded American prevailing 6-3 7-6 (7-2) 5-7 6-2 in the final at Flushing Meadows.

Zverev added the New York title to his collection after winning the French Open earlier this year. In a bizarre ending, Shelton's return sailed long on match point, but Zverev, seemingly unaware that he had won, hit the balls back to the other end of the court, ready for another game.

It was only when Zverev glanced up at the big screen that he realised he had actually won.

"I feel like there was so much suffering for the Zverev family at Grand Slam level, that maybe 2026 is the year we should just enjoy," Zverev told Sky Sports Tennis . "Everything is going perfectly. I am unbelievably happy.

"Three months ago if I was told you are going to win one Grand Slam in your career and nothing else, I would have signed the paper straight away and never questioned it.

"Now standing here with two Grand Slam trophies in the space of the months is incredible."

And on not realising he had won it on Championship point, he admitted: "I thought the score was 5-1! I knew that I had broken him twice, but I thought he only held once.

"I was thinking: 'Okay, I'm going to have a relaxed service game here and then I'll get tight on the next one.' "It was lucky for me!

"It's actually funny, teachers in tennis say play each point and forget about the score. Well I forgot about the score and it helped me!"

Shelton was bidding to become the first American man to win a Grand Slam singles title since Andy Roddick in 2003, while also aiming to become only the second black man to triumph at this level after Arthur Ashe in 1975. He walked onto the court to a rapturous reception from a partisan crowd of 23,000 spectators inside the stadium named in Ashe's honour.

Among the star-studded crowd were actors Brad Pitt and Rami Malek, as well as James Bond star Pierce Brosnan, who received a mischievous camera shot from the TV director with the match clock showing just 0.07.

Despite spending 19 hours and 38 minutes on court en route to the final - the fourth-longest total recorded by a player reaching a Grand Slam final since 1991 - Zverev made a blistering start. He broke in the opening game and then broke again on set point to seize control.

Shelton could not even earn a break point in the opening two sets, as Zverev, the No 1 seed at a Grand Slam for the first time, relied on his powerful serve to keep the American at bay.

Shelton had lost all five of his previous meetings with Zverev, but he had also arrived in New York having never beaten Stefanos Tsitsipas or, most notably, Carlos Alcaraz - until this tournament. That run gave him plenty of reason for optimism heading into Sunday's final at Flushing Meadows.

But Zverev, now playing with freedom after shedding the unwanted tag of the 'best player never to win a major' with his French Open triumph earlier this year, dominated the second-set tie-break to move within a set of the title.

Shelton dug in, to his credit, and finally brought up three break - and set - points as the Zverev serve suddenly faltered, and the crowd were in full voice again when he converted the second.

But the match was effectively over as a contest when Zverev, who has capitalised on the fitness struggles and absences of Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner at various points this year, broke early in the fourth set.

His incessant ball-bouncing - statistics showed he spent around three hours of his 23-plus hours on court this fortnight bouncing the ball between serves - finally resulted in a time violation.

But the 29-year-old held his nerve to clinch Grand Slam title No 2, and his first in New York, in three hours and 33 minutes. After a brief pause to take it all in, he finally began to celebrate.

Shortly after his victory, Zverev reserved his most heartfelt thanks for his mother Irina, a former professional tennis player, crediting her with ​refusing to let type 1 diabetes dictate his future.

"When your four-year-old son is diagnosed ⁠with diabetes and doctors in the office tell you ⁠that life and sports will be very limited for that child, it takes a very strong mother to say 'my son will be whatever he wants ‌to be'," Zverev said.

"If he wants to be a tennis player, he'll be a tennis player. If he wants to do something else, he'll do something else but this illness will not define us.

"I'm happy ‌that we worked through it and we're doing things that we're doing right now. My mother is the most important and strongest person I know because it takes an unbelievably strong woman to do what she did."

Zverev also paid tribute to Shelton, saying: "Ben, you're an incredible player and an incredible person.

"This was your first Grand Slam final but I already told you you're going ​to be back here many more times and if I would have to bet all my money on it, I would bet that you would lift this ‌trophy one day."

Shelton, who was not even a year old the last time an American man won a Grand Slam title, said: "Sascha, congrats on these two weeks, your second Grand Slam title and two in one year.

"What you're doing is incredible, the way you are serving and moving in play. You work harder than anyone I know, and do more hours on court than anyone else.

"You and your team do things the right way and I'm sincerely happy for you guys to hold this title.

"To New York, you guys drove me here today. I'm just getting started and I'll be back here again."

Henman: Zverev has transformed from a player who was going backwards a year ago

"The perseverance and the way Zverev's game has improved over the last 12 months," said the former British No 1.

"I was looking back at his Grand Slam results, and his game was going backwards.

"But he has transformed himself to be more aggressive, and when you reflect on this matchup, Zverev had beaten Shelton five times in a row.

"Shelton had to change the narrative, but Zverev looked so comfortable.

"Shelton did a great job getting that third set, but losing his serve first game of the fourth settled Zverev down and gave him more energy. He coasted to the line from there."

Bartoli: Difference in experience was massive factor

"The difference in their experience was absolutely massive," said the former Wimbledon champion.

"When you look at the first game of the final, Ben Shelton won the toss, elected to serve, fell to 30-30, missed an easy shot and then double faulted to give away the first break straight away.

"Look, it's not easy to come out in front of your home crowd and play your first ever Grand Slam final in those circumstances.

"Of course you have all the crowd for you, but you want to please them at the same time, put on a show and play your best tennis.

"Zverev made only one unforced error in the first set, and it just made Shelton's life so difficult.

"There's no shame losing to Zverev when Zverev is playing like this."

Zverev viaja con su padre Alexander, que hace las funciones de entrenador.

articles.title: Six years after 2020 heartbreak, Alexander Zverev beats Ben Shelton to finally win US Open
articles.summary: Tennis News: Alexander Zverev finally got his hands on the US Open trophy that once seemed destined to be his, overcoming American hope and his own painful Grand S.
articles.body: Alexander Zverev finally got his hands on the US Open trophy that once seemed destined to be his, overcoming American hope and his own painful Grand Slam history to beat Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6(2), 5-7, 6-2 in Sunday’s final at Flushing Meadows.Six years after blowing a two-set lead against Dominic Thiem in the 2020 US Open final, Zverev completed one of the biggest pieces of unfinished business in his career. The German, who became a Grand Slam champion at Roland Garros earlier this year, added a second major title in New York to cap a remarkable 2026 season.“I think God has seen how hard we worked, how much we suffered, how much pain we went through and I think 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before,” Zverev said during the trophy presentation.The victory also ended an extraordinary run of disappointment in Grand Slam finals for Zverev, who had previously reached the championship match at the US Open in 2020 and the French Open in 2024 before finally breaking through in Paris this year.Zverev silences partisan New York crowdThe home crowd had been desperate to see Shelton end a 23-year wait for an American man’s Grand Slam title. The eighth seed was attempting to become the first American man to win a major since Andy Roddick at the 2003 US Open and the first Black American man to win the title since Arthur Ashe in 1968.But Zverev refused to be intimidated by the partisan atmosphere.“I know that today 99.9% of the people wanted Ben to win so I'm very sorry,” Zverev said. “Even though I know that the crowd was against me, the crowd was always incredibly fair and we as players we appreciate it.”The German made the perfect start, capitalising on Shelton’s nerves in his first Grand Slam final. Shelton double-faulted on break point in the opening game and Zverev held his advantage throughout the set, closing it out when the American committed another double fault.Zverev’s composure became even more evident in the second set. With the crowd attempting to lift Shelton and occasionally reacting loudly to Zverev’s mistakes, the top seed remained focused and raced through the tiebreak, taking a 5-0 lead before closing it 7-2.Shelton fights back but Zverev refuses to crackShelton, however, refused to surrender.Zverev looked on course for a straight-sets victory after saving a break point with a stunning backhand winner in the sixth game of the third set. Shelton then slipped and crashed to the court, but the setback appeared to galvanise him.The American began finding greater depth and power from the baseline, eventually breaking Zverev for the first and only time in the match. He held his nerve to take the third set 7-5 and send the final into a fourth.But the comeback ended there.Zverev immediately broke Shelton’s serve at the start of the fourth set and then survived a 25-shot rally to strengthen his grip on the match. The German never relinquished the advantage, eventually closing out the contest 6-2.In an almost surreal moment, Zverev initially did not realise he had won. After Shelton sent a return long on match point, Zverev instinctively moved back towards the baseline as if preparing to receive another serve.Only after the umpire announced, “Game, set and match Zverev”, and the crowd rose to applaud, did the German realise the title was his. He smiled, raised his arms and headed to the net to embrace Shelton.From 2020 heartbreak to 2026 gloryThe triumph erased one of the most painful chapters of Zverev’s career. In 2020, he led Thiem by two sets and came within two points of victory before becoming the first man since 1949 to lose a Grand Slam final after taking the opening two sets.This time, there was no collapse.Zverev has now gone 25-2 in Grand Slam matches in 2026, having won the French Open, reached the Wimbledon final and followed that run by claiming his second major title in New York.He also collected a record $5.5 million winner’s prize, matching women’s champion Elena Rybakina’s payout from Saturday as the biggest prize in Grand Slam history.Shelton, meanwhile, leaves New York with a breakthrough of his own despite falling short. He had stunned defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set quarter-final that ended at 3:33 a.m., but could not complete the ultimate upset.“You’re one of the very best players in the world, maybe the best player in the world this year,” Shelton told Zverev.For Zverev, there was no better way to answer the ghosts of 2020 than by finally lifting the US Open trophy.“We went 30 years without winning a Slam title and now won two in the span of three months,” he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Ben Shelton isn’t the men’s American tennis hero – yet
articles.summary: Shelton’s megawatt smile and a made-for-social-media aura made him the darling of the NY crowd at the US Open, but the young American wasn’t ready for the moment… yet.
articles.body: After Ben Shelton beat countryman Frances Tiafoe in a historic semifinal, he marveled at the star power that had come to Arthur Ashe to witness his win. “I keep looking up at the screen like oh shoot, Jalen Brunson is here,” he said in his post-match comments on the court to the audible delight of the crowd. Shelton has a baby face and a seemingly unshakable cockiness, the combination of which lent this compliment an added dose of aw shucks, awe-struck, game-recognizing-game. There was a bevy of, perhaps, bigger celebrities in attendance - Brunson was seated next to Ben Stiller, for instance. But Shelton’s comments reflected the post-NBA-Finals reality in New York (or, at least, a savvy awareness of how to pander to it). The Knicks are sports royalty in this city. Winning does that. On Sunday, the packed crowd for the US Open men’s final was eager, at times to the point of collective desperation, to elevate Shelton himself to a similar status. It would have made him the first American man to win the Open or, indeed, any Grand Slam championship since Andy Roddick in 2003. He would have been the first Black man to win a Grand Slam title since the stadium’s namesake did so 51 years ago at Wimbledon. He had enjoyed a storybook run through the tournament to get to this stage. The No. 9 ranked player had prevailed in a semis that was the first ever to feature two Black American men. Before that, he dispatched the seven-time Grand Slam winner Carlos Alcaraz in an epic match that ended after 3:30 a.m. This would be his first ever Grand Slam final. His dad is his coach. His girlfriend is a famous soccer star who traveled 250 miles from her own game in D.C. on Sunday to make it to his match. Of course the 23-year-old with a megawatt smile and a made-for-social-media aura was the darling of the Queens crowd. And as much as the many thousands of New Yorkers wanted to see Shelton prevail – This is your house! someone yelled at one point; I love you, Ben! another added – they also wanted to see the No. 2 ranked German, Alexander Zverev, lose. They booed his stumbles and egged on his faults, repeatedly calling for One more! in hopes of seeing a double fault. It’s impossible to know, of course, how much of that animosity was nonspecific patriotism and how much, if any, was a direct response to the allegations of domestic violence made against Zverev by two of his former partners. The 29-year-old was never convicted, but nor was he proven innocent. One former partner declined to bring any criminal or civil charges against Zverev; the other, the mother of his child, settled with him out of court. If that seems like an awkward or abrupt departure for a tennis story, that’s because it is. Zverev’s new level of success this season – he finally shed the official title of best player to never win a Slam title at the French Open a few months ago – has re-centered the uncomfortable, unfortunate, but un-ignorable and all-too-common complexity of personal misconduct in sports. Athletes are not always aspirational. On the one hand, that’s not their job. On the other hand, shouldn’t it be? Rootability isn’t ranked or quantified. It’s quaint, but it’s also what keeps the sport – any sport – viable. I don’t blame anyone who couldn’t bring themselves to root for Zverev. And a desire for collective rooting is what packed Arthur Ashe on Sunday. So they rooted for Shelton to author an upset. And it would have been one. In addition to occupying the higher seed, Zverev has prevailed in all five of their previous meetings. Shelton managed to win just one set in that span. He would win just one more on Sunday, falling 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2 to his superior opponent. That third set, though, that animated the stadium. The DJ played Estelle’s ‘American Boy’ between games. The crowd chanted USA! When he clinched the set, Shelton cupped his ear to call for the standing ovation to revel even louder and they were happy to oblige. It felt like the momentum had shifted. Or maybe that’s just the storyteller in me talking. Shelton, though, is no author. And he’s not yet the best tennis player he can be. Maybe if there was a little more magic in the world, he would have won the US Open anyway, taking advantage of a field without Jannik Sinner and an injury-compromised Alcarez to end the drought of American male winners. In truth, Shelton isn’t ready. “Walking out on that court today, there’s nothing like it. I’ve never felt anything like that before,” he said appreciatively in his post-match press conference. That was about the energy, the atmosphere, a build-up to an obvious desire to return to such a heady state and an illustrious stage. A few minutes later, he inadvertently found a different angle on the newness of it all. This is the furthest he’s ever made it in a Grand Slam. The most high-level tennis he’s ever played in a two-week span. “I was tired before I took the court today,” Shelton said. Maybe Ben Shelton is the future of American men in tennis. Maybe that future is a bright one. If the magic had been there for the men’s final of the US Open, maybe he would have inspired a new generation of boys to take up a racquet and a renewed national interest in a sport currently dominated on the men’s side by Europeans. Instead, on the first NFL Sunday of the season, the kid who was his middle school quarterback came in second. In the media dining room, Zverev’s triumphant press conference was muted while the US Open staff watched football with the sound on. No new heroes in the Knicks’ New York.

articles.title: Watch: Alexander Zverev didn’t realise he had won the US Open — until the crowd told him
articles.summary: Tennis News: Alexander Zverev had waited six years to erase the pain of his 2020 US Open final defeat. When the moment finally arrived at Flushing Meadows on Sunda.
articles.body: Alexander Zverev had waited six years to erase the pain of his 2020 US Open final defeat. When the moment finally arrived at Flushing Meadows on Sunday, the German almost missed it.The No. 1 seed defeated American Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6(2), 5-7, 6-2 to win his first US Open title and complete a remarkable Grand Slam season. But it was the bizarre aftermath of the winning point that quickly went viral.Zverev's hilarious winning momentZverev served for the championship at 5-2 in the fourth set. Shelton sent the return long, and the match was over. Yet Zverev did not immediately react.Instead, the German moved back behind the baseline as though he was preparing for the next point. There was no immediate fist pump, no leap and no arms raised in celebration.It was only when the crowd rose to its feet and the huge ovation made the situation sink in that Zverev realised he had just won the US Open.He then raised his arms, smiled and finally celebrated the victory he had chased for so long.The official US Open account shared the moment on social media with the caption: “HE DIDN'T REALIZE HE'D WON”, alongside the message that Zverev had “exorcised his 2020 demons” by defeating Shelton.The unusual celebration offered a striking contrast to the emotional significance of the victory.Watch:From 2020 heartbreak to two-time Grand Slam championSix years earlier, Zverev had been just two points from winning his maiden Grand Slam title against Dominic Thiem in New York. He led by two sets and even served for the championship before suffering a devastating five-set defeat.That loss remained one of the defining scars of his career.But after winning the French Open earlier this year, Zverev said the wounds from that 2020 defeat had finally disappeared.“The scars of the 2020 (U.S. Open) final, they disappeared after I won in Paris,” Zverev said. “I said at Wimbledon, though I lost in the final, I enjoyed the match ... enjoyed playing on Centre Court in front of an amazing crowd.”The German has now turned a season of Grand Slam opportunities into his best year at the biggest tournaments. He won the French Open, reached the Wimbledon final and finished with a second major title after triumphing in New York.Zverev improved to 25-2 in Grand Slam matches in 2026 and collected $5.5 million for his US Open triumph.‘2026 is the outcome of all the years’While the victory was a personal breakthrough, Zverev also credited his family and team for helping him reach the summit.He paid an emotional tribute to his mother Irina, a former professional tennis player, for refusing to allow his type 1 diabetes diagnosis at the age of four to dictate his future.“When your 4-year-old son is diagnosed with diabetes and doctors in the office tell you that life and sports will be very limited for that child, it takes a very strong mother to say 'my son will be whatever he wants to be',” Zverev said.He also thanked his father Alexander Zverev Sr and brother Mischa, before reflecting on the long journey behind his second major title.“We went almost 30 years without winning a Grand Slam title and now we've won two in a span of three months,” he said.“I think God has seen how hard we've worked, how much we've suffered, how much pain we went through and I think that 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before.”For Shelton, meanwhile, the defeat extended the wait for an American men's Grand Slam champion. articles.summary: "Hemos hecho muchos sacrificios el uno por el otro y viajado por el mundo para apoyarnos mutuamente"
articles.body: Trinity Rodman, delantera de las Washington Spirit (NWSL) y novia del tenista Ben Shelton, se ha convertido en una de las grandes protagonistas del US Open y en el "talismán" del tenista estadounidense que ha disputado su primera final de un Gran Slam. La futbolista mejor pagada del mundo, que es hija del mito de la NBA Dennis Rodman (con el que no mantiene una buena relación), ha apoyado al tenista estadounidense durante su final en el US Open y le ha acompañado durante todo el torneo (llegó a lucir una camiseta con el lema "amo a mi novio"). Tras perder la final del US Open el emergente Ben Shelton, que sucumbió por 6-3, 7-6(2), 5-7 y 6-2 en 3 horas y 33 minutos ante el alemán Alexander Zverev, dijo sobre Trinity Rodman que "significa todo". "Sabía que iba a ser casi imposible que llegara, pero el simple hecho de hacer el esfuerzo e intentarlo es increíble". Llegó justo cuando estaba perdiendo, lo cual seguro fue una decepción para ella...", apuntó Shelton, recordando que Trinity llegó a Nueva York tras jugar con la Spirit un partido de la NWSL que su equipo perdió 0-3 contra las Boston Legacy. Ben Shelton comentó sobre su relación con Trinity Rodman, a la que hizo llorar de emoción durante su discurso, que "hemos hecho muchos sacrificios el uno por el otro y viajado por el mundo para apoyarnos mutuamente". "Este es mi lugar feliz. Este es el lugar donde más me gusta estar y ojalá este torneo no terminara nunca... "Esta derrota duele mucho", aseguró Shelton en su discurso como finalista. El propio Zverev se dirigió a Trinity Rodman tras ganar a Shelton: "Trinity, creía que hoy tenías partido, ¿no? Felicidades a ti también. Eres el talismán. Hoy no, pero normalmente sí".
